items.prompt: Which best describes org-level influence?
choices: Winning a single meeting by persuading the people in the room that day
Shaping many later decisions you won't attend
Getting your own manager to approve one particular request
items.explanation: Org-level influence is about the many smaller decisions made later, elsewhere, without you.

items.prompt: At org level, what does winning look like?
choices: The room applauds your presentation
The vote goes your way on the day
Your position becomes the default
items.explanation: There is no vote, so the win is the position becoming the default choice.

items.prompt: Where does org-level influence mostly show up?
choices: In writing, cited by people who never spoke to you
In one meeting room at one moment in time
In private chats with your own manager only
items.explanation: Decisions happen where you are absent, so the written trail does the work.

items.prompt: What is the typical time horizon of org-level influence?
choices: A single afternoon of focused work
Months to years
Days to a couple of weeks
items.explanation: Many separate decisions happen on their own schedules, so it plays out slowly.

items.prompt: What is the main tool for a single-decision problem?
choices: A written document that someone finds years from now
A reputation that compounds over a long career
A coalition built before the meeting
items.explanation: A single decision has one moment, so the work is lining up support before it.

items.prompt: Why does one strong fifteen-minute pitch not settle Yuki's problem?
choices: Real decisions come later, team by team, without her
Pitches are not allowed at architecture reviews
Tech leads cannot follow technical arguments
items.explanation: A pitch is one input; it is not the moment anything gets decided.

items.prompt: How many decisions does Yuki's goal actually depend on?
choices: One, made by a single senior executive
Fourteen separate ones, made by different tech leads on their own schedules
None, because nobody is really deciding
items.explanation: Each team decides on its own, whenever it starts or restructures a service.

items.prompt: Which problem has a clear single moment where it gets decided?
choices: An org-level problem spread across many teams
A long-run reputation-building problem
A single-decision problem
items.explanation: Single-decision problems have one meeting or sign-off; org-level problems do not.

items.prompt: A director wants every team in a 12-team department to adopt a shared review checklist. Nobody will vote on it; each team changes its own habits whenever it likes. Which description fits her problem?
choices: An org-level problem: success means the checklist becomes a changed default that each team reaches on its own schedule
A single-decision problem, since one person signs off on the template and that is the moment that matters
A single-decision problem, since announcing it once at a department meeting completes the work for every team
Not an influence problem, since nobody is voting against it and nobody needs persuading
items.explanation: No vote and many independent adopters mean the goal is a changed default, not one outcome. An announcement reaches the room, not the later team-level choices.
items.reference:
Two kinds of problem
single: one room, one day, a coalition
org-level: many decisions, no room, you absent
win = your position becomes the default
Why: at org level the decisions happen later and elsewhere, so what you leave behind has to do the persuading.
items.learnMore:
Single moment vs. policy

A single decision is a sprint with a deadline. Org-level influence is closer to setting a policy that has to survive dozens of decisions you will never attend.

Common mistake

Treating a good pitch as the finish line. A pitch reaches the room; the decisions arrive later, one team at a time.
items.reflection: Think of a change you wanted in a group you did not manage. Was there ever a single moment it was decided, or many small ones?

items.prompt: Dev won a migration vote by lining up allies for one meeting. Yuki tries the same recipe for service boundaries: she gets 14 tech leads into one room and wins a show of hands. A year later, 3 of 14 services follow it. What best explains the gap?
choices: The vote was too narrow, so the fix is to hold a larger vote with more executives present in the room
Tech leads who vote yes deliberately break their promises later to protect their own autonomy
A show of hands binds only the room, while later decisions are made alone, under pressure, with no reminder of the vote
Votes only work for decisions about hardware, not for decisions about how software is designed
items.explanation: A meeting outcome fades; decisions made months later need the reasoning findable at that moment.

items.explanation: One is a sprint toward a deadline, the other is closer to setting a policy that outlives any moment.

choices: Treat the talk as the decision moment and push for a spoken commitment from everyone present
Decline the invitation, since talks have no effect on org-level influence and spend her budget
Spend all fifteen minutes on her own track record so the room trusts her judgment from then on
Use it to point people to a findable document they can cite later

items.prompt: Which is a durable artifact?
choices: A written RFC or design doc
A hallway conversation
A private message to one person
items.explanation: It is written down so it keeps working after the conversation ends.

items.prompt: What is reputation, in this unit?
choices: How loudly someone argues
Trust earned by being visibly right over a long stretch of time
A job title on a profile
items.explanation: People defer to a record, not to one strong argument.

items.prompt: What is seeding?
choices: Forcing a decision in the meeting itself
Hiding an idea until the very last day
Introducing an idea before it is needed
items.explanation: Seeding makes an idea familiar early, so it feels like confirming later.

items.prompt: What is an influence budget?
choices: The finite time and credibility you have
Money set aside for a conference
A list of people you plan to avoid
items.explanation: Hours and trust are limited, so they must be spent deliberately.

items.prompt: What is a company-wide bet?
choices: Any opinion you happen to hold about the codebase
A direction chosen on purpose
A prediction about how the stock will do next year
items.explanation: A bet is picked deliberately; an opinion is just something you have.

items.prompt: Why can a written document persuade when its author is absent?
choices: It forces people to obey
It replaces every conversation
It carries the reasoning to people who never met the author
items.explanation: The reasoning travels with the document, so a stranger can apply it.

items.prompt: Which tool makes an idea feel familiar before the decision arrives?
choices: Seeding, done early and lightly
A mandate handed down from a manager
A tight deadline
items.explanation: Seeding places the idea early, in low-stakes spots.

items.prompt: Which tool limits how many things you can push at once?
choices: A durable artifact that anyone can read
The influence budget
Seeding done in several different places
items.explanation: Hours and credibility run out, which caps how many bets can be funded.

items.prompt: Yuki wants a team she has never spoken to to follow her service-boundary guidance six months from now. Which tool is doing the work at the exact moment that team decides?
choices: Her influence budget, which pays for the hours she spends in that team's meetings
Seeding alone, because a familiar idea needs no written support when the decision arrives
A durable artifact that a stranger can find and cite at that moment, without her there to explain it
A mandate, because titles bind teams in all of their later decisions without any follow-up
items.explanation: Only the artifact is present at the moment of decision; the others prepare the ground or limit the effort.
items.reference:
The four tools
📄 artifact: reasoning that outlives the talk
📈 reputation: a record people can check
🌱 seeding: familiar before it is needed
⏳ budget: finite hours and credibility
Why: each tool covers a different gap: findability, trust, timing, and capacity.
items.learnMore:
Four tools, four gaps

Artifacts solve findability, reputation solves trust, seeding solves timing, and the budget solves capacity. A plan that uses only one leaves the others as weak points.

Common mistake

Assuming one great document is enough. Without trust, timing, and spare hours, even a strong document can sit unused.
items.reflection: Which of the four tools do you already lean on at work, and which one do you tend to forget?

items.prompt: A tech lead reads Yuki's RFC and distrusts it because they do not know her. Years later, after two of her warnings proved accurate, they adopt her next RFC quickly. Which tool changed?
choices: Reputation: her record gave the same kind of document more weight with a reader who had not met her
Seeding: the idea had already been mentioned in several earlier design reviews and retros
The budget: she suddenly had far more spare hours to spend on the second document
The artifact: the second RFC was simply longer and more detailed than the first one was
items.explanation: Same author and kind of document, different trust. A visible record is what shifted.

items.prompt: Which can a stranger find and cite later?
choices: A hallway chat
A comment spoken in a meeting
A written RFC linked from a wiki page
items.explanation: Written, linked material can be found; a spoken remark cannot.

items.prompt: What should a durable artifact always include?
choices: The reasoning, including rejected alternatives
Only the final verdict
The author's job title
items.explanation: The why lets others extend the rule to new cases.

items.prompt: Why is 'Yuki told me once' weak support?
choices: Yuki is always wrong when speaking
A third party can't check it
Spoken words are never allowed as evidence
items.explanation: A stranger needs something they can read for themselves.

items.prompt: What does a verdict with no reasoning cause?
choices: Instant universal agreement across all the teams involved
A better reputation for the author of the rule
Inconsistent following in new cases
items.explanation: Without the why, people cannot tell whether a new case counts.

items.prompt: Does an artifact work without its author present?
choices: Yes, the reasoning stands alone
No, the author must read it aloud
Only on the day it is published
items.explanation: That is the point: it keeps persuading in her absence.

items.prompt: What is an ADR?
choices: A type of meeting room
A short record of a design decision and why it was made
A tool for measuring uptime
items.explanation: ADR stands for architecture decision record.

items.prompt: A message in a busy chat channel is mostly:
choices: Permanent and easy to search
Required reading for the whole company
Buried in scrollback within days
items.explanation: Chat is fast to write and fast to lose.

items.prompt: The job of a durable artifact is mainly to:
choices: Carry reasoning to people who never met the author
Announce that the author won
Replace later conversations
items.explanation: It exists so a stranger can apply the logic correctly.

items.prompt: Two rules are published. Doc A: 'Each service owns its data.' Doc B: the same rule plus the incidents behind it, two rejected alternatives, and a section on when it does not apply. A new case appears that neither doc mentions. What is most likely?
choices: Readers of A are safer, since a short rule leaves less room for misreading it in new situations
Readers of B can reason about the case; readers of A tend to treat it as out of scope
Both groups decide the same way, since the rule itself is worded identically in both documents
Readers of B hesitate longer, because the extra detail makes the rule look optional to them
items.explanation: The reasoning is what lets a reader extend the rule to something unlisted.
items.reference:
Message vs. artifact
chat: buried, uncitable, needs the author
artifact: findable, citable, stands alone
include the why and rejected options
Why: the artifact's job is to carry reasoning far enough that a stranger can apply it to a case you never imagined.
items.learnMore:
Why reasoning matters more than the rule

A rule only covers cases that look like its example. The reasoning behind it, plus the alternatives that were rejected, is what lets someone handle the case you did not write down.

Common mistake

Writing a forceful verdict and calling it done. Without the why, readers either follow it too literally or skip it when a case looks different.
items.reflection: Think of a rule at work you only half understand. What would the author have needed to write for you to apply it correctly to a new case?

New tech leads dislike meeting senior engineers in person and tend to avoid the session
It breaks when she is unavailable, and no third party can cite what she said live
items.explanation: A live explanation depends on her presence; the written reasoning does not.

items.prompt: What builds reputation, as used here?
choices: One very forceful argument
A long and impressive job title
A visible record of being right
items.explanation: Trust accumulates from past calls that people can check.

items.prompt: Can one great presentation replace a track record?
choices: No, trust compounds slowly over many calls
Yes, if it is delivered loudly enough
Yes, as long as the slides are thorough
items.explanation: A single event cannot stand in for repeated visible results.

items.prompt: What happens when you are wrong in public on your own topic?
choices: Your trust grows even faster than before
Some of your trust is spent
Nothing ever changes
items.explanation: Misses draw down the same account that your good calls fill.

items.prompt: Is reputation best thought of as topic-specific?
choices: No, it applies equally to every subject you touch
No, it only exists inside one meeting
Yes, tied to where the record was built
items.explanation: Strong in one area does not make an expert in another.

items.prompt: What does a visible correct warning do?
choices: Gives your next claim more benefit of the doubt
Makes people stop reading
Resets your record to zero
items.explanation: Each correct call makes the next one easier to believe.

items.prompt: Confident opinions outside your expertise tend to:
choices: Add to your reputation
Spend credibility you may need later
Be ignored without any cost
items.explanation: They risk a public miss on a topic where you have no standing.

items.prompt: Reputation compounds. What does that mean?
choices: It doubles every month without any effort
It only applies inside a single meeting
Early wins ease later claims
items.explanation: Past trust lowers the effort needed to be believed next time.

items.prompt: Who can shortcut building a reputation?
choices: Nobody; it takes time and results
Anyone who prepares a good slide deck
Anyone who holds a senior title
items.explanation: No single piece of evidence replaces a record built over time.

items.prompt: Yuki has a strong record on service boundaries. Which move most likely draws down trust she needs for those bets?
choices: Saying 'I have not worked on that, so treat this as a guess'
Declining to comment on a topic she has not studied
Publishing a careful RFC on her specialty after months of review
Giving a confident verdict in an area with no track record
items.explanation: Confidence without standing is the one that risks a visible miss on a different topic.
items.reference:
The trust account
deposit: a warning that proved accurate
deposit: a design that held up
withdrawal: confident claims outside your record
withdrawal: defending a miss past the evidence
Why: trust is built from a visible record and spent by misses and overreach, so it has to be used on the bets that matter.
items.learnMore:
Being right is not being trusted

People rarely verify everything. A record of correct calls shortens how much checking they do on the next one, which is why it compounds and why it cannot be rushed.

Common mistake

Treating reputation as general authority. It is closer to topic-specific credibility, so an overconfident answer elsewhere spends it for little gain.
items.reflection: Whose judgment do you trust without checking, and what record earned that? Where would you not extend the same trust?

items.prompt: Two engineers make the same correct prediction. One has been right on three earlier calls in that area; the other has no history. A manager must decide whether to act before verifying. Which is more likely to be acted on quickly?
choices: The second, because newer voices are assumed to carry fewer biases than established ones
The first, because past visible accuracy shortens how much checking the claim gets before action
Both equally, since a correct claim wins on its merits before anyone looks at the speaker
Neither, since a manager never acts on a prediction before it has been fully verified
items.explanation: Trust shortens the checking people do; it does not change whether the claim is true.

items.prompt: When is a new idea hardest to introduce?

Mid-decision, under time pressure
During a quiet, relaxed chat
items.explanation: A half-formed plan under pressure treats a new idea as a detour.

Familiarity ahead of time

Only after the decision is made

items.prompt: What shape does the curve have?

Rises, peaks, then falls
Always falls with more bets
items.explanation: Landed bets increase until budget runs thin, then decline.

items.prompt: Using the unit's model (120 hours a year, about 30 needed per bet), how do three bets compare with six?
choices: Six give about twice as many as three, since there are twice as many attempts to land
They give the same number, since the total hours spent are identical in both cases
Three give about 2.55 landed bets; six give about 2.27, since each of six gets only 20 hours

items.explanation: Six bets get 20 hours each, below the 30 needed, so more attempts produce fewer wins.
items.reference:

120 hrs/year, ~30 hrs per bet
peak near 4 bets, then it declines
8 bets: ~15 hrs each, most fall short
Why: landed bets rise only while each still gets enough sustained hours, then more attempts produce fewer wins.
items.learnMore:
A threshold, not a slope

Below a certain number of sustained hours, a bet does not become a durable default at all. That is why the curve turns down instead of just flattening.

Common mistake

Treating attention as divisible without loss. Splitting the same hours across more bets can drop each below the point where it works.

Wait quietly until the discussion fades from view, then continue as if nothing had been said

durable artifact = visible discussion
credible critique: acknowledge, revise
weak critique: brief respectful reply
silence reads as no answer
